regions.name: Mashhad district (Nader Mirza 1796-1803; Salar revolt 1848-50)
regions.geometry_note: Mashhad county plus Binalud. Nader Mirza and Hasan Khan Salar each held the shrine city; neither man's wider reach is mappable to counties (see i_salar_khorasan_wide). Modern Mashhad county is far larger than the 19th-century city+oasis.

regions.name: Sabzevar-Neyshabur zone held by Hasan Khan Salar (1848-49)
regions.geometry_note: Sources only name Sabzevar and Neyshabur (Nishapur) as retaken by the government in March 1849; the neighbouring counties are inferred. Wikipedia also lists Bojnurd and Qa'en as dominated by Salar; those belong to separate regions (i_bojnurd_shadlu, i_qaenat_alam) and are omitted to avoid overlap.

regions.name: Torbat-e Heydarieh (Qara'i principality)
regions.geometry_note: Iranica: a Qara'i principality "stretching from the gates of Mashhad to Khaf" with Torbat-e Heydarieh as capital. Counties are an approximation of that corridor; the real boundary fluctuated with the chiefs' power.

regions.name: Quchan (Za'faranlu Kurdish ilkhanate)
regions.geometry_note: Za'faranlu Kurds held Quchan/Chenaran (Iranica names Chenaran as their seat in the Qajar period). Faruj and Dargaz are approximations of their pastoral range on the Atrek/Kopet-Dag side.

regions.name: Bojnurd-Esfarayen (Shadlu Kurdish ilkhanate)
regions.geometry_note: Iranica: Shadlu controlled Esfarayen and Bojnurd; Kurds of other tribes (Keyvanlu, Bicaranlu, Zangalanlu...) held the remainder of northern Khorasan. Counties are the modern North Khorasan block minus Quchan-side units.

regions.name: Qa'enat (Khozeimeh/'Alam amirate)
regions.geometry_note: Core Qa'enat districts of modern South Khorasan. Tabas/Ferdows/Boshruyeh were at times attached to the Qa'enat governorship but are left out. Sistan is separate (i_sistan).

regions.name: Tabas (hereditary Zangu'i/Vakil khans)
regions.geometry_note: Tabas county only; the historical Tabas-e Masina/Gilaki governorship may have reached Ferdows/Boshruyeh margins, not mapped.

regions.name: Sistan (Persian Sistan)
regions.geometry_note: Modern Iranian Sistan = the 1872 Goldsmid award line (west of the Helmand). Before 1872 the Sistan lowlands were ruled by local chiefs and disputed with Afghanistan; the Iranian county set is only the part that ended up in Iran.

regions.name: Persian Baluchistan: Bampur, Fahraj, Sarbaz, Dizzak, Saravan
regions.name_fa: بلوچستان (بمپور، فهرج، سرباز، دیزک و سراوان)
regions.geometry_note: Western/central Baluchistan, the domain of the Bampur governorate and the Barakzai (Baranzai) chiefs. Counties approximate old districts Bampur, Dizzak, Sarbaz, Geh and Qasr-e Qand named by Iranica.

regions.name: Sarhad (Khash, Mirjaveh, Zahedan/Dozdab)
regions.geometry_note: Northern Baluch highland (Sarhad) along the British Baluchistan frontier; the Dozdab (Zahedan) railhead lies in Zahedan county. Boundary with the Bampur block approximate.

regions.name: Chabahar bay (Omani dependency until 1872)
regions.geometry_note: Only the Chabahar-Dashtiari coast was concerned. The two modern counties are much larger than the Omani-claimed bay and its Jadgal-controlled hinterland.

regions.name: Khorasan under Col. Pesyan (1921)
regions.geometry_note: Razavi Khorasan minus the Quchan/Dargaz Kurdish zone (which fought Pesyan). Wikipedia calls the entity the Autonomous Government of Khorasan with Mashhad as capital; actual reach beyond Mashhad, Neyshabur and Sabzevar is poorly documented.

regions.name: Turkmen Sahra (Yomut and Goklen)
regions.geometry_note: Plain between the Atrek, the Caspian shore and the Gorgan river. Yomut lived west/south of Gonbad, Goklen to the east; Galikash/Minudasht/Azadshahr were mixed or Persian-settled and are omitted. Tribal ranges were seasonal and fuzzy.

regions.name: Shahsevan country (Ardabil, Moghan, Sabalan)
regions.geometry_note: Winter pastures in Moghan (Parsabad, Bilehsavar, Garmi) and summer pastures on the Sabalan slopes (Meshkinshahr, Ardebil, Khalkhal) = modern Ardabil Province. Shahsevan also ranged into Sarab (East Azerbaijan; left out to avoid overlap with Azadistan) and, per Iranica, between Zanjan and Qazvin; only the core block is mapped.

regions.name: Gilan
regions.geometry_note: Whole of modern Gilan province. Jangali control (1915-20) was concentrated in Fuman, Shaft, Siahkal, Rasht hinterland, Lahijan and Rudbar; the coast (Anzali, Rasht) was repeatedly held by Russian/British garrisons or the Soviets, so single-province treatment is a simplification.

regions.name: Tabriz and the Jolfa road
regions.geometry_note: Russian garrisons held Tabriz and the Julfa-Tabriz axis; the 1908-09 siege concerned the Tabriz city and its quarters. Modern Tabriz county is larger than the 1909 city.

regions.name: Azadistan (Khiabani) - East Azerbaijan
regions.geometry_note: Khiabani's movement claimed the whole province of Azerbaijan; Iranica says only a few towns stayed under Tehran or tribal chiefs, but only Tabriz's control is firmly documented. East Azerbaijan is used as the maximum plausible extent.

regions.name: Urmia-Khoy-Salmas plain
regions.geometry_note: Counties around Lake Urmia's west shore that saw the Russian withdrawal (1918), the Assyrian-Kurdish war and the Ottoman reoccupation (June-July 1918).

regions.name: Ottoman-occupied frontier strip west of Lake Urmia (1906-12)

custom.description: A strip about 25-40 km wide along the Iran-Ottoman border from south-west of Sauj Bulaq to west of Khoy; clip the union of within_units to the polygon.
custom.note: Polygon is schematic: sources name Behik (Baradost), Dasht, Mergever, Sardasht, Bana, Ganjachin, Baradost and later Mergever (Aug 1907) and a strip "from south-west of Sauj Bulaq to west of Khoy". Not surveyed.

regions.geometry_note: Schematic strip; see custom.note. A county-union would grossly overstate the occupation.

regions.name: Azerbaijan occupied by Russia (1827-28) except Khoy
regions.geometry_note: Tabriz (13 Oct 1827), Urmia (28 Jan 1828), Ardabil (8 Feb 1828) are the documented captures; Marand/Jolfa (the Aras crossing and road), Khoy and Salmas are inferred as lying on the Russian line. The Turkmenchay treaty tied evacuation to indemnity instalments, so the occupied area shrank by stages. Verification: Khoy split off to i_russian_khoy_1828, which Russia kept as security for the indemnity long after the rest of Azerbaijan was evacuated.

regions.name: Qazvin-Zanjan sector of Norperforce
regions.geometry_note: Norperforce had its HQ at Qazvin, the main body at Manjil (Gilan, inside i_gilan), a battalion at Zanjan and posts along the Manjil-Qazvin road. The occupation was a road-line, not a full area.

regions.name: Sanandaj / Ardalan Kurdistan (and southern Kurdistan in 1979-83)
regions.geometry_note: Modern Kurdistan Province. The Ardalan vilayet centred on Sanandaj (Senneh) and Bijar, Kamyaran, Marivan, Sarvabad; Saqqez and Baneh were Mukri/Ardalan marchland and are the least certain inclusions for 1800-67.

regions.name: Paveh-Javanrud-Ravansar (Kermanshah Kurdistan, 1979-83)
regions.geometry_note: Kurdish-majority counties of Kermanshah province in which Kurdish forces took garrisons in March 1979 and fought in Aug-Sept 1979.

regions.name: Mahabad zone (Mukriyan; Republic of Mahabad; KDPI core)
regions.geometry_note: Mukriyan = south of Lake Urmia incl. Mahabad, Bukan, Sardasht, Oshnaviyeh. The 1946 republic is usually described as Mahabad, Bukan, Naghadeh, Piranshahr, Oshnavieh, with Sardasht often added. Miandoab was Azeri-majority and contested; it is left out here and put under ADP.

regions.name: Area overrun by Sheikh Ubeydullah (1880)
regions.name_fa: مناطق تصرف‌شده به دست شیخ عبیدالله (۱۲۵۹)
regions.geometry_note: Sources say Sauj Bulaq (Mahabad) and Maragheh were taken and Urmia held out; Miandoab lies between them. Raiding extended widely west of Lake Urmia, but held ground is not mappable.

regions.name: Shikak country (Simko), Salmas-Chehriq-Ushnu
regions.geometry_note: Chehriq fortress (Salmas county) was Simko's base; Qotur/Baradost/Ushnu and the Mamash/Mangur/Piran pastures are covered by the neighbouring counties. Extent varied month to month.

regions.name: Mahabad-Miandoab sector under Simko (1921-22)
regions.name_fa: مهاباد، بوکان و میاندوآب در دورهٔ سمیتقو
regions.geometry_note: Wikipedia (single source) credits Simko with Mahabad (Sauj Bulaq) from Oct 1921; control of Miandoab/Naghadeh is less certain.

regions.name: Kalhor-Guran-Sanjabi border Kurds (Kermanshah frontier)
regions.geometry_note: Iranica: under Davud Khan Kalhor "absolute master of the entire territory between Kermanshah and the Ottoman border", also subjecting Guran and Sanjabi. Counties approximate this border belt.

regions.name: Kermanshah plain and Hamadan road (Kermanshah, Sahneh, Harsin, Kangavar, Sonqor)
regions.geometry_note: Core Kermanshah-Sahneh-Bisotun-Harsin corridor that Russian, Ottoman and British forces fought over in 1915-18; the border-belt counties (Qasr-e Shirin etc.) are in i_kalhor_border_kurds.

regions.name: Hamadan province
regions.geometry_note: Modern Hamadan province; Hamadan city and the Hamadan-Kermanshah and Hamadan-Qazvin roads are what was occupied.

regions.name: Luristan (Pish-e Kuh)
regions.geometry_note: Modern Lorestan province. The Pish-e Kuh Lur tribes (Bala Gariveh, Dirakvand, Silakhor, Selseleh, Bayravand...) ranged over this block; the towns of Khorramabad and Borujerd had Qajar governors but the highlands did not obey them.

regions.name: Pusht-e Kuh (Ilam; walis)
regions.geometry_note: Iranica lists Ayvan, Sirvan-Chardavol, Ilam, Darreh Shahr, Mehran and Abdanan as Pusht-e Kuh, with Dehloran sometimes included.

regions.name: Bakhtiari country (Chahar Mahal and eastern Khuzestan)
regions.geometry_note: Summer quarters (yaylaq) in Chahar Mahal and the Zagros crest, winter quarters (qeshlaq) in the Khuzestan piedmont (Masjed Soleyman, Izeh, Lali, Andika, Baghmalek). Fereydan/Fereydunshahr and Semirom fringes and the Khuzestan lowland ranges are excluded.

regions.name: Kohgiluyeh, Boir Ahmad and Mamasani
regions.geometry_note: Six tribal groups of Kuhgiluya; Boir Ahmad is the largest. Mamasani/Rostam (Fars) joined them under Emamqoli Khan against Reza Shah. The lowland market town Behbahan (Khuzestan) and the Gachsaran/Dogonbadan piedmont fringe are only partly covered; Behbahan is deliberately left out to avoid overlap with the Khuzestan occupation block.

regions.name: Qashqai range (Fars)
regions.geometry_note: Qashqai winter quarters in Firuzabad, Farashband, Kazerun and the Gulf-side Qir/Karzin; summer quarters round Semirom, Eqlid, Abadeh and Sepidan. Migration routes crossed Shiraz county. The range was seasonal and overlapped other tribes (Khamseh, Mamasani).

regions.name: Mohammerah (Khorramshahr) and Abadan island
regions.geometry_note: Seat of the Muhaysin/Ka'b sheikhs. Modern county boundaries are larger than the 19th-century sheikhdom nucleus.

regions.name: Fallahiyeh (Shadegan), Hendijan, Mahshahr, Ramshir
regions.geometry_note: The Ka'b heartland (Fallahiyeh=Shadegan) and the Khaz'al estates granted in 1903 (Fallahiyeh, Hendijan, Deh Molla, Mashur).

regions.name: Northern Khuzestan placed under Khaz'al (1907-24)
regions.name_fa: شمال خوزستان در قلمرو شیخ خزعل
regions.geometry_note: Iranica: from 1907 Khaz'al administered northern Khuzestan; by 1911 "most of the country" was under the sheikh except Dezful and Shushtar. Counties are inferred.

regions.name: Bandar Lengeh and dependencies (Qawasim)
regions.geometry_note: Port of Lengeh and its dependent coast (Charak/Mogh, in Parsian county). Qasimi dependencies on islands (Abu Musa, Tunbs, Sirri) were handled by the frontier researcher.

regions.name: Bastak (hereditary khans)
regions.geometry_note: Hereditary Khans of Bastak governed the Bastak/Irahistan district under the governor of Fars/Lar.

regions.name: Larestan (Lar, Gerash, Evaz, Khonj)
regions.geometry_note: Area ruled by Sayyed Abd al-Hosayn Lari 1909-15; extent between Lar town, Gerash, Khonj and Lamerd inferred from contemporary descriptions.

regions.name: Tangestan, Dashtestan and Dashti (Bushehr hinterland)
regions.geometry_note: Tribal districts behind Bushehr; khans of Tangestan (Zair Khidr, Shaikh Hosein Khan of Chah Kutah), Dashtestan and Dashti are the actors.

regions.name: Bushehr port and county
regions.geometry_note: Bushehr county includes the port, Reshire and, administratively, Kharg island; Kharg has its own circle region.

regions.name: Kharg island

custom.description: Island of Kharg, about 8 km long.
custom.note: Island inside Bushehr county; use a circle or the island polygon.

regions.geometry_note: Small island; circle approximates its outline.

regions.name: Basidu (west tip of Qeshm island)

custom.description: British station site at Basidu, west end of Qeshm island.

regions.geometry_note: Station and depot at the west end of Qeshm; British claims never covered the whole island.

regions.name: Henjam (Hengam) island
regions.geometry_note: Small island; circle approximates it.

regions.name: Ashurada island (Gorgan Bay)

custom.description: Ashurada islands at the tip of Miankaleh peninsula, Gorgan Bay.
custom.note: Inside Mazandaran/Golestan coastal border; use island polygon.

regions.geometry_note: Small island group; circle approximates it.

regions.name: Bandar Abbas, Minab-Khamir coast, Qeshm and Hormuz (Omani lease)
regions.name_fa: بندرعباس، میناب، خمیر، قشم و هرمز (اجارهٔ عمان)
regions.geometry_note: Iranica: a coastal strip of about 150 km from Minab in the east to Khamir in the west, plus the islands of Qeshm and Hormuz, and inland about 30 miles in some British accounts. County units over-extend inland; Hormuz is inside Bandar-e Abbas county.

regions.name: South Persia Rifles base at Bandar Abbas (1916-21)

custom.description: Bandar Abbas garrison town (circle) rather than a whole county.
custom.note: Sykes landed here in March 1916; Kerman and Shiraz are now separate regions because the SPR reached them months later (i_spr_kerman, i_spr_shiraz).

regions.geometry_note: Circle approximation only. Verification: the original single region covered Shiraz, Kerman and Bandar Abbas from March 1916, but Sykes reached Kerman on 12 June 1916 and Shiraz on 11 Nov 1916, so those towns were split into i_spr_kerman and i_spr_shiraz.

regions.name: Isfahan (Bakhtiari constitutionalists, 1909)
regions.geometry_note: The two Isfahan keys in the catalog (city-level and surrounding county) are used; their relationship is unclear and may double-cover the same area.

regions.name: Khorramshahr (Iraqi occupation 1980-82)
regions.geometry_note: The Iraqi bridgehead covered the city and the eastern bank of the Shatt; the whole county is shown.

regions.name: Abadan island (siege 1980-81)
regions.geometry_note: Abadan was besieged but the city and refinery stayed in Iranian hands; Iraqi forces took parts of the north/west of the island and the Bahmanshir bank.

regions.name: Susangerd-Bostan-Hoveyzeh plain (Iraqi occupation 1980-82)
regions.geometry_note: Iraqi forces held Bostan and parts of Dasht-e Azadegan; exact holdings varied (Iran liberated Bostan 29 Nov-7 Dec 1981, but Iraqi forces still held ground near Susangerd).

regions.name: Qasr-e Shirin-Sarpol-e Zahab-Gilan-e Gharb-Dehloran (Iraqi occupation 1980-82)
regions.name_fa: قصرشیرین، سرپل ذهاب، گیلان غرب و دهلران
regions.geometry_note: Iraq entered 20-40 km deep on this front (Qasr-e Shirin 20 km, Dehloran 30 km according to later accounts); counties overstate the depth.

regions.name: Mehran
regions.geometry_note: Mehran changed hands several times (1980, 1986, 1988); the county is shown whole although the occupation was of the town and its approaches.

regions.name: Iraqi-held border pockets after the 1988 ceasefire (to Aug 1990)
regions.name_fa: نوار مرزی در اشغال عراق پس از آتش‌بس

custom.description: A strip about 15 km wide along the international border within the listed counties.
custom.note: Contemporary reports (Aug 1990) cite about 2,600 km2 / 1,000 sq mi of Iranian land still held by Iraq; the locations were not identified in sources found, so the strip is schematic.

regions.geometry_note: Schematic; do not render as full counties.

regions.name: Soviet zone of Azerbaijan (ADP area)
regions.name_fa: آذربایجان در منطقهٔ اشغال شوروی (حکومت پیشه‌وری)
regions.geometry_note: East and West Azerbaijan (minus the Mahabad-republic counties), Ardabil and Zanjan. Zanjan's inclusion in the ADP is from general accounts; the Democrats' writ in the south of the area (Zanjan, Takab, Miandoab) was thinner and was cut off by the Iranian army before reaching Tabriz.

regions.name: Soviet-occupied north (Gilan, Mazandaran, Golestan, Qazvin)
regions.name_fa: شمال در اشغال شوروی (گیلان، مازندران، گلستان، قزوین، سمنان)
regions.geometry_note: Gilan, Mazandaran and Gorgan are named in the sources; Qazvin (southern outpost of the Soviet line) and Semnan are inferred. Soviet garrisons were concentrated in towns and along the roads; Iranian civil administration continued. (Verification: Semnan province was split out to i_wwii_soviet_semnan because the Soviets left Mashhad/Shahrud/Semnan in March 1946, earlier than the rest.)

regions.name: Soviet-occupied Khorasan (1941-43)
regions.geometry_note: Iranica: Soviet troops took Mashhad and Bojnurd and "occupied all of Khorasan" until winter 1943; the south (Birjand etc.) is not included.

regions.name: British-occupied south and west (1941-46)
regions.name_fa: جنوب و غرب در اشغال بریتانیا
regions.geometry_note: The British entered Khuzestan, Kermanshah and Hamadan in Aug-Sept 1941 and held the Persian Corridor from the Gulf to Hamadan. Paiforce garrisons later reached Isfahan, Shiraz and the Gulf ports, but Fars (Qashqai/Khamseh range, treated separately), Hormozgan and the east are NOT included because British control there was thin or absent. Only a schematic block. Verification: Sanandaj county (IRN2_227) added - British and Soviet columns met at Sanandaj on 30 Aug 1941 and 'southern Kurdistan up to Sanandaj' fell in the British zone (low confidence; the Kurdish-held belt from Mahabad to Saqqez lay between the zones). The wider extent of the British zone (Fars, Isfahan, Kerman, Hormozgan) was not established.

regions.name: Soviet-occupied Semnan province (1941-46)
regions.geometry_note: Semnan province counties (Shahrud, Damghan, Semnan, Garmsar etc.), split out of i_wwii_soviet_north. Sources say the Soviets held Shahrud and Semnan until March 1946; the extent south to Garmsar is inferred from the Soviet advance to Qazvin/Tehran and the Mashhad road.

regions.name: Khoy (Russian-held pledge, 1828)
regions.geometry_note: Khoy county. Under Turkmenchay Russia evacuated Azerbaijan except Khoy, which it held as a deposit until the indemnity was paid; modern Khoy county is larger than the 1828 district.

regions.name: Shiraz (pro-German Gendarmerie, 1915-16)

custom.description: Shiraz city and its immediate surroundings.
custom.note: The gendarmes and Democrats held the city; the countryside was held by tribal forces on both sides.

regions.geometry_note: Circle round Shiraz city; the surrounding Fars countryside was divided among Qashqai, Khamseh and Tangestani forces.

regions.name: Zanjan town (Babi revolt, 1850-51)

custom.note: Only part of the town (Hujjat's quarters) was Babi-held; a county-union would grossly overstate.

regions.geometry_note: Circle round Zanjan town; the divided town cannot be mapped more finely.

regions.name: Abadan island (British garrison, 1914-18)
regions.geometry_note: Abadan county stands in for the island refinery zone; the British perimeter did not cover the whole county.

regions.name: South Persia Rifles garrison at Kerman (1916-21)
regions.geometry_note: Circle approximation of the garrison town.

regions.name: South Persia Rifles garrison at Shiraz (1916-21)

custom.note: Garrison town only; the force did not control the Qashqai/Khamseh countryside.

regions.geometry_note: Circle approximation of the garrison town.

defacto.controller: Imperial Russia (Caspian naval station; Soviet Russia to 1921)
defacto.note: Following a Persian request for ships against Turkmen raiders (Iranica: 1254/1838), Russia built barracks and stationed warships on Ashurada; Iranica ('Gorgan vii') places the occupation in Mohammad Shah's reign (1834-48). Wikipedia gives 1837 and Qajar-era sources 1841; the earlier 1842 start was too late. Russians recognised Iranian sovereignty but refused to evacuate and returned the islands under the Persian-Soviet treaty of Feb 1921 (Iranica dates this to 13 Feb 1921; the treaty was signed 26 Feb 1921).
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Āšūrāda' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/asurada/)
Wikipedia, 'Ashuradeh' (cross-check; 1837 / 1841 variants)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Gorgān vii. History from the Safavids to the end of the Pahlavi era' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/gorgan-vii/)

defacto.controller: Sheikh Mohammad Khiabani and the Democratic Party of Azerbaijan ("Azadistan")
defacto.note: Khiabani's armed supporters took Tabriz on 7 April 1920 (Swedish-officered police left; bazaar closed 9 April) and proclaimed Azadistan as a model of free government against the 1919 Anglo-Persian Agreement; he considered himself an Iranian nationalist, not a separatist. Cossack forces entered Tabriz on 14 Sept 1920 and Khiabani was killed. Only Tabriz's control is firmly documented. Persian-language sources used by Wikipedia ('Mohammad Khiabani's uprising') date the start to 5 April 1920; Iranica has 7 April.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Ḵiābāni, Shaikh Moḥammad' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/%E1%B8%B5iabani-shaikh-mo%E1%B8%A5ammad/)
Wikipedia, 'Russian occupation of Tabriz' (cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915)
Wikipedia, 'Mohammad Khiabani's uprising' (cross-check; 5 Apr - 14 Sept 1920)

defacto.controller: Bakhtiari ilkhani/ilbegi families (Chahar Lang supremacy to 1841; Haft Lang ilkhanis from Hosein Qoli Khan, 1867; Sardar As'ad, Samsam al-Saltaneh)
defacto.note: Bakhtiari khans were the semi-autonomous overlords of Chahar Mahal and the Khuzestan piedmont and, in 1909, helped depose Mohammad Ali Shah and thereafter held ministries and governorates. Reza Shah detribalised them: ilkhani/ilbegi titles abolished 1933, khans arrested and some executed in 1934, territory divided 1936. The 1929-31 Bakhtiari revolt (9 July 1931 in Isfahan province) did not hold territory for a month.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Baḵtīārī' articles incl. 'Baḵtīārī tribe', 'Esfandīār Khan', 'Baktiari ii' (iranicaonline.org) [search extracts]
Wikipedia, 'Persian tribal uprisings of 1929' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Baluch sardars of Bampur, Dizzak, Sarbaz, Geh and Qasr-e Qand (with Kalat and Muscat influence)
defacto.note: Iranica: the province was "practically independent" until Persian troops occupied Bampur in 1849.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Baluchistan i. Geography, History and Ethnography' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/baluchistan-index/baluchistan-i/) [search extract]

defacto.controller: Persian governor at Bampur (Sartip Ebrahim Khan) with local rulers paying taxes; later the Barakzai (Baranzai) chiefs Mir Bahram Khan (d. 1921) and Dost Mohammad Khan (1921-28)
defacto.note: Bampur was garrisoned permanently from 1850; Kerman's governor campaigned against Baluch tribes in 1862. Persian influence waned after 1905; Dost Mohammad, recognised as governor of Bampur in 1921, claimed autonomy until Gen. Jahanbani's 1928 campaign; he later escaped from Tehran and was hanged on 16 Jan 1930. End month is an estimate. After the 1928-29 campaign the Iranian state continued to govern Persian Baluchistan through Iranian-appointed local sardars (Jan-Mohammad Buledi at Qasr-e Qand, Mehrab Khan Bozorgzadeh at Jaleq, Mohammadshah Mir-Moradzay at Sib, Shahbaz Khan Bozorgzadeh at Dizzak - Wikipedia 'Dost Mohammad Khan Baloch'); that quasi-indirect phase is NOT mapped here (no end date established), so the renderer shows direct control after 1928.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Baluchistan i. Geography, History and Ethnography' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/baluchistan-index/baluchistan-i/) [search extract]
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kerman ix. History in the Qajar Period' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kerman-09-qajar-period/)
Wikipedia, 'Dost Mohammad Khan Baloch' (cross-check)
Koyagi, M., 'Tribes and Smugglers in Iran's Eastern Borderlands, 1921-41', Iranian Studies (Cambridge UP, 2021), pp. 405-422
Wikipedia, 'Dost Mohammad Khan Baloch' (cross-check; post-1928 appointed sardars)

defacto.controller: Baluch tribes of Sarhad (Rigi, Ismailzai, Damani, Baranzai) under their sardars
defacto.note: Iranica: Persian Baluchistan was 'practically independent' until Persian troops occupied Bampur in 1849/50; Sarhad lay beyond even that. Frontier demarcated 1895-96.
sources: Koyagi, M., 'Tribes and Smugglers in Iran's Eastern Borderlands, 1921-41', Iranian Studies (Cambridge UP, 2021), pp. 405-422
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Baluchistan i. Geography, History and Ethnography' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/baluchistan-index/baluchistan-i/) [search extract]
Gazetteer of Persia vol. IV (Government of India, c.1908-10), via Qatar Digital Library (qdl.qa) [search extract]

defacto.controller: British India (Seistan Force detachments, then Sarhad Levy Corps with a garrison at Khash)
defacto.note: British troops were stationed at Khash from May 1916 and organised tribal levies; after the 1920 Sistan withdrawal they stayed. The "official ceremony ending the British occupation of Iranian Baluchistan" was held on 1 March 1924, when the Union Jack at Khash was replaced by the Iranian tricolour.
sources: Koyagi, M., 'Tribes and Smugglers in Iran's Eastern Borderlands, 1921-41', Iranian Studies (Cambridge UP, 2021), pp. 405-422
Wikipedia, 'Seistan Force' (cross-check; formation July 1915, Seistan Force from March 1916, last elements out Nov 1920)

defacto.controller: Iranian military command (Salar Amjad) paying subsidies to Baluch chiefs; Dost Mohammad Khan claiming autonomy
defacto.note: Tehran took over the subsidy-and-levy arrangement; control rested on chiefs such as the Rigi chief Idu Khan. Campaigns against Dost Mohammad culminated in 1928.
sources: Koyagi, M., 'Tribes and Smugglers in Iran's Eastern Borderlands, 1921-41', Iranian Studies (Cambridge UP, 2021), pp. 405-422
Wikipedia, 'Dost Mohammad Khan Baloch' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Britain (Bombay Marine/Government of India station; sepoy detachment)
defacto.note: After the General Treaty of Peace (1820) Basidu became the main British operational base in the Gulf (until about 1863); a sepoy detachment stayed to 1879, after which only a coal depot under a native agent remained until the depot moved to Henjam in 1911-12. Persian protests and claims over Qeshm never lapsed.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Qešm Island' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/qeshm-island/)

defacto.controller: Hereditary Khans of Bastak (Sheikh Mohammad Khan Bastaki in the 18th century; later Mohammad-Reza Khan and his father, titled Sowlat al-Molk)
defacto.note: The Khans of Bastak governed the district and, as late as 1854, controlled Lengeh's Qasimi sheikh (revenue collector under the governor of Bastak); a Fars governor's force from Lar captured Bastak in 1809. From 1856 the governorship of Lengeh itself went to outsiders and in 1887 Persia ended the Qasimi governorship, but that does NOT end the Bastak khans: Persian Gulf Residency monthly reports of 1912-20 (file 2297/1919) still show the Khan of Bastak (Mohammad-Reza Khan) and his father contending for the Lengeh administration, so the researcher's 1887 end was too early. The new end, 1925, is still a placeholder tied to Reza Khan's consolidation in the south; the real date was not found.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bandar Lengeh' (Sheikh of Lengeh as revenue collector under the governor of Bastak, to at least 1854; cross-check)
Persian Gulf Residency Monthly Reports 1912-20, File 2297/1919 (Khan of Bastak and the Lengeh administration), via Qatar Digital Library [search extract]
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kholosi' (mentions the khans of Bastak) [search extract]

defacto.controller: Shadlu Kurdish ilkhanis (Ebrahim Khan; Najaf-Ali Khan, ilkhani from 1802; Sardar Mo'azzaz Bojnurdi in 1921)
defacto.note: Shadlu and other Kurdish tribes ran Bojnurd and Esfarayen; they were the force that killed Col. Pesyan in 1921. Bombing of Bojnurd on 18 May 1925 marked the collapse; forced settlement from 1929; the last Kurdish ilkhan (Faraj-Allah Khan Bicaranlu) failed to seize power in 1942. Iranica adds that in spring 1925 the Kurds of Bojnurd were 'apparently under the control of the central government' (acting against Turkmen besiegers of Bojnurd) and that from about 1925 the ilkhani system collapsed; on 16 Feb 1942 Faraj-Allah Khan Bicaranlu briefly seized Shirvan, Esfarayen, Darreh Gaz, Mane, Samalqan, Jajarm, Faruj and Quchan before being defeated (under a month; not mapped).
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Khorasan xvii. The Kurdish Communities of Khorasan' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/khorasan-xvii-the-kurdish-communities-of-khorasan/)

defacto.controller: Britain (Indian Army expeditionary force; Gen. Outram from 27 Jan 1857)
defacto.note: Bushehr surrendered on 9-10 Dec 1856 after the storming of Reshire (5 Dec); Borazjan was occupied 5 Feb 1857. Iranica says the British evacuated the Gulf by mid-1857; Wikipedia gives October 1857 for Bushehr.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Anglo-Persian War (1856-57)' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/anglo-persian-war-1856-57/)
Wikipedia, 'Anglo-Persian War' (cross-check; Bushehr evacuated Oct 1857)

defacto.controller: Britain (Maj. A. P. Trevor, military commander)
defacto.note: British forces took Bushehr on 8 Aug 1915 after the 12 July attack on the Residency, disarmed the gendarmerie and raised the Union Jack; the occupation ended by agreement on 16 Oct 1915 (Persian postal authority regained 18 Oct), and the British returned in 1916 with the SPR.
sources: Wikipedia, 'British occupation of Bushehr' (8 Aug - 16 Oct 1915; cross-check)
Wikipedia, 'Rais-Ali Delvari' and 'British occupation of Bushehr' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Sultanate of Muscat and Oman (Chabahar as a Makran/Gwadar appanage, held through Jadgal chiefs such as Din Muhammad of Dashtiari)
defacto.note: Lorimer: Chahbar remained an appanage of Oman until 1872. In January 1872 'Abd al-'Aziz, brother of Sultan Turki, seized it; in March a Persian army expelled him (the Persian governor of Bampur, Sartip Ebrahim Khan, had asserted that Chahbar belonged to Persia). Actual Omani presence before 1872 was nominal and mediated by local chiefs.
sources: Lorimer, Gazetteer of the Persian Gulf (1915), via Qatar Digital Library (qdl.qa), entry on Chahbar 1872 [search extract]

defacto.controller: Constitutionalist forces at Rasht (Sepahdar Tonekaboni, Mo'azzed al-Saltaneh) against Mohammad Ali Shah
defacto.note: Rasht fell to the constitutionalists in January 1909 and became a base from which a Gilani force marched on Tehran, which fell on 13 July 1909. They rejected the shah's government rather than seeking separation. Month of the Rasht takeover is approximate.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Russia i. Russo-Iranian Relations up to the Bolshevik Revolution' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/russia-i-relations/)
Not independently verified in this research pass; reconstructed from general scholarship

defacto.controller: Imperial Russian garrisons at Anzali and Rasht
defacto.note: Russia landed troops at Anzali in April 1909 and, with Persian administration continuing, kept troops in Gilan until its evacuation in Jan-Mar 1918. The date of first occupation of Rasht itself is not fixed.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Russia i. Russo-Iranian Relations up to the Bolshevik Revolution' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/russia-i-relations/)

defacto.controller: Jangalis (Mirza Kuchek Khan) vs. Russian, British (Dunsterforce, Norperforce) and Qajar forces
defacto.note: Kuchek Khan took to the forests in October 1915; after the Russian Revolution the Jangalis ran much of Gilan's administration (1917), signed an agreement with Dunsterforce (Aug 1918, Manjil battle), were dispersed by a British-Qajar offensive in March 1919 and regrouped by summer. Russian garrisons left in early 1918; British posts (Anzali) until May 1920.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Jangali movement' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/jangali-movement/)
FIBIS wiki, 'Norperforce' (wiki.fibis.org/w/Norperforce)

defacto.controller: Persian Socialist Soviet Republic (Kuchek Khan, Ehsanollah Khan, Haydar Khan Amu-oghlu) under Red Army protection
defacto.note: The Red Army landed at Anzali on 18 May 1920; the Soviet Republic of Gilan was proclaimed at Rasht on 4-6 June. After the Feb 1921 Persian-Soviet treaty the Red Army left on 8 Sept 1921 and Reza Khan's forces took Rasht in October; Kuchek died in December 1921.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Jangali movement' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/jangali-movement/)
Wikipedia, 'Persian Socialist Soviet Republic' (cross-check; Red Army withdrawal 8 Sept 1921)

defacto.controller: Imperial Russia (Baratov column)
defacto.note: Baratov took Hamadan in December 1915 (sources: 3 or 15 Dec). The Russians evacuated it on 9 Aug 1916 (last troops marched out that afternoon) and the Ottoman XIII Corps entered on 10 Aug 1916 (Segal 2023, citing A.C. Edwards, an eyewitness).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)
Wikipedia, 'Kermanshah operation' (cross-check; Russian entry to Kermanshah 26 Feb 1916)

defacto.controller: Ottoman Empire (XIII Corps, Ali Ihsan)
defacto.note: Ottoman XIII Corps entered Hamadan on 10 Aug 1916 while Baratov's Russians held the Sultan Bulagh pass about 75 miles from Qazvin. The Ottoman advance halted at the end of its supply line; the sources consulted (Wikipedia 'Persian campaign (World War I)', citing Caven) have Baratov moving on Hamadan again in December 1916, and Hamadan changed hands that month. This replaces the researcher's undated 'contested' status Aug 1916-Mar 1917; the end month is the weakest part (some accounts keep the Ottomans there into early 1917).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)
Segal, J. E., Journal of Russian American Studies 7.2 (2023) [Ottoman entry 10 Aug 1916; Russian line at Sultan Bulagh]

defacto.controller: Imperial Russia (Baratov corps, disintegrating)
defacto.note: Russian garrisons (Baratov's Caucasian Cavalry Corps) re-entered Hamadan in December 1916 and held it until the army dissolved in winter 1917-18. Start moved from 1917-03 to 1916-12 (see the Ottoman record above); low confidence.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Russia i. Russo-Iranian Relations up to the Bolshevik Revolution' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/russia-i-relations/)

defacto.controller: British (Dunsterforce, then Norperforce lines)
defacto.note: Dunsterville's advance party reached Hamadan in Feb 1918; the British kept Hamadan as a base on the Kermanshah-Qazvin line until Norperforce left on 21 April 1921.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Dunsterforce' (cross-check)
FIBIS wiki, 'Norperforce' (wiki.fibis.org/w/Norperforce)

defacto.controller: Britain (Royal Navy/Government of India coaling depot and naval base)
defacto.note: A telegraph station had been tolerated since the late 1860s; the coaling depot moved from Basidu to Henjam in 1911/12 and by 1913 it was the main British naval base. Persia had granted only a telegraph concession; Reza Shah demanded evacuation and the British abandoned the station in 1935.
sources: Qatar Digital Library, 'British Naval Bases in the Gulf, 1820-1935: A History of Tensions' (qdl.qa) [search extract]

defacto.controller: Iran (defenders) vs. Iraq (besiegers)
defacto.note: Iraqi forces encircled Abadan from late 1980 but never took the city; the siege was lifted on 27 Sept 1981 (Operation Samen-ol-A'emeh). Start date is the invasion date; full encirclement came later.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Iraq vii. Iran-Iraq War' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iraq-vii-iran-iraq-war/)

defacto.controller: Iraq
defacto.note: Iraq entered Dehloran, Qasr-e Shirin, Sumar, Naft Shahr, Sar-e Pol-e Zahab and Mousiyan on 12 July 1988 and withdrew from the towns after Iran accepted the ceasefire; but reports in August 1990 say Iraq still held about 2,600 km2 (1,000 sq mi) of Iranian territory, which it began to evacuate on 16-17 Aug 1990 (a UN report of 24 Sept 1990 said withdrawal was almost complete). Locations of the pockets were not identified in sources found. Verification: UNIIMOG's own background says that by end-September 1990 withdrawal to the international boundaries was 'almost complete' with a few locations where forces of each side were still on the wrong side, and that by end-January 1991 Iraq had withdrawn from 23 of 29 disputed positions (Iran from 13 of 17). The pockets were therefore a handful of border positions, not a large contiguous area, and the Aug 1990 '2,600 km2' figure comes from press reports of Saddam Hussein's offer. Record kept at low confidence.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Tawakalna ala Allah Operations' (cross-check; Iraqi entry to Dehloran/Qasr-e Shirin 12 July 1988)

defacto.controller: Iraq
defacto.note: The Iraqi attack on Khorramshahr began on 22 Sept 1980; the city fell on 24 Oct (Iraqi control effectively complete 10 Nov) after a 34-day battle and was liberated on 24 May 1982 in Operation Beit ol-Moqaddas. Iraq announced its withdrawal from remaining Iranian territory on 20 June 1982.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Iraq vii. Iran-Iraq War' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iraq-vii-iran-iraq-war/)

defacto.controller: Iraq vs. Iran (Mehran changed hands several times)
defacto.note: Iraq captured Mehran in the 1980 invasion; Wikipedia ('Battle of Mehran (1986)') calls the May 1986 capture the third time Iraq took it, so Iraqi control before 1986 was not continuous, and the Mehran article says the Iraqis had been driven out by 1982-83. Dates of the first recapture are not established, so the whole span is coded contested (low) instead of the researcher's continuous foreign occupation to June 1982.

defacto.controller: Iraq (II Corps)
defacto.note: Iraq recaptured Mehran on 15-19 May 1986 ("for the third time"); Iran retook the area in Operation Karbala-1 (30 June-3 July 1986) and defeated a Republican Guard counter-attack on 4 July.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Mehran (1986)' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Iraqi forces with the Mojahedin-e Khalq (Operation Forty Stars)
defacto.note: On 18 June 1988 Iraq and the MEK crushed two Iranian divisions and seized Mehran; Iraqi regulars left after three days and the MEK stayed. Wikipedia says Iran retook Mehran in Operation Mersad (26 July); the end date is uncertain.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Operation Forty Stars' and 'Operation Mersad' (cross-check; dates of Mehran 1988 uncertain)

defacto.controller: Iraq
defacto.note: Iraqi forces held Bostan and parts of the Dasht-e Azadegan plain (the Susangerd salient). Iran relieved a siege of Susangerd in Nov 1980 and recaptured Bostan and 70 villages on 29 Nov-7 Dec 1981 (Operation Tariq al-Quds); the rest was cleared by June 1982. Holdings varied by month. Verification (Iranica 'Iraq vii'): after Fath ol-Mobin (22 March 1982, Shush-Dezful) and the 22 March offensive north of Bostan, the stage of 24 April-12 May 1982 'drove the Iraqi troops back to Khorramshahr from the Ahvaz-Susangird area'; the end is therefore moved from 1982-06 (the date of Iraq's general withdrawal announcement) to 1982-05. Khorramshahr itself (separate record) fell on 24-25 May.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Operation Tariq al-Quds' and 'Liberation of Susangerd' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Iraq
defacto.note: Iraq took Qasr-e Shirin on the first days of the invasion and advanced on the Kermanshah and Ilam fronts (Sar-e Pol-e Zahab, Gilan-e Gharb, Musian/Dehloran); the central-front lines were pushed back in Dec 1981-Jan 1982 and Iraq announced its withdrawal on 20 June 1982. Town-by-town dates are not established here.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Iraq vii. Iran-Iraq War' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iraq-vii-iran-iraq-war/)
Wikipedia, 'Tawakalna ala Allah Operations' (cross-check; Iraqi entry to Dehloran/Qasr-e Shirin 12 July 1988)

defacto.controller: Bakhtiari constitutionalist khans (Samsam al-Saltaneh, Sardar As'ad)
defacto.note: Bakhtiari forces took Isfahan in early 1909 and, with Sardar As'ad (who entered the city on 14 May 1909 per Iranica), marched on Tehran with the Gilan force, which fell on 13 July 1909. Dates are approximate.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Baḵtīārī' articles incl. 'Baḵtīārī tribe', 'Esfandīār Khan', 'Baktiari ii' (iranicaonline.org) [search extracts]
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Russia i. Russo-Iranian Relations up to the Bolshevik Revolution' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/russia-i-relations/)

defacto.controller: Kalhor chiefs (Davud Khan, killed 1912 fighting for Salar al-Dowleh; his successor Abbas Khan), with Guran and Sanjabi subordinate
defacto.note: Iranica: Davud Khan Kalhor, who 'ruled the tribe in the early 1900s', started as a peddler and made himself 'the absolute master of the entire territory between Kermanshah and the Ottoman border', also subjugating the Guran and Sanjabi; he held the Qajar title Sardar-e Mozaffar and governed the Kalhor district. He was killed fighting for Salar al-Dowleh (1911 per British records and Wikipedia; 1912 per Iranica) and his successor Abbas Khan was imprisoned by Reza Shah in 1926. CORRECTION: the researcher's 1800 start is dropped. Before c.1900 the Kalhor were one of several tribes inside the province of Kermanshah, governed from the city by Qajar princes (Kalhor and Zangana levies served those governors, e.g. against the Bakhtiari in 1830), with no autonomous Kalhor ruler; those years are left as direct. The exact start of Davud Khan's ascendancy (c.1900) is approximate.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kalhor' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kalhor/) [search extract]
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kermanshah iv. History to 1953' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kermanshah-04-history-to-1953/)

defacto.controller: Salar al-Dowleh (Abolfath Mirza) with Kalhor, Jaf, Sanjabi and Lur followers vs. Bakhtiari/government forces
defacto.note: Mohammad Ali Shah's brother occupied Sanandaj by 17 July 1911, seized Kermanshah (given up to plunder) and, per Wikipedia, Hamadan; he marched on Tehran, won a first battle near Malayer and was decisively beaten near Saveh by Amir Mofakham Bakhtiari (his Kalhor ally Davud Khan died in this campaign: 1911 per the British records and Wikipedia, 1912 per Iranica). The revolt did not end there: he remained in the Kermanshah-Kurdistan area until Farman Farma's 1912 expedition (Persian Gulf Administration Report 1911-14: 'In July Salar-ed-Dowleh fled from Kermanshah, on the arrival of Farman Farma ... and left for Luristan and Kurdistan'), so the end is moved from Dec 1911 to July 1912. Control of each town in between is not established; status stays contested.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kermanshah iv. History to 1953' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kermanshah-04-history-to-1953/)

defacto.controller: Committee for the Defence of Iran's Independence / National (Provisional) Government of Kermanshah under Nezam al-Saltaneh Mafi, backed by German and Ottoman agents
defacto.note: Nationalists left Tehran for Qom (Nov 1915) and set up an anti-Allied government at Kermanshah; Ottoman and German forces occupied the city in 1915-16. The government fell back before the Russian entry on 26 Feb 1916.
sources: University of Edinburgh thesis abstract, 'Muhajirat and the National Government of Kermanshah, 1915-1917' (era.ed.ac.uk) [search extract]

defacto.controller: Imperial Russian Caucasian Cavalry Corps (Gen. Baratov)
defacto.note: Russian forces broke through at Sahneh (22 Feb), took Bisotun (24 Feb) and entered Kermanshah on 26 Feb 1916; the Ottoman XIII Corps (Ali Ihsan) retook it on 2 July 1916.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Kermanshah operation' (cross-check; Russian entry to Kermanshah 26 Feb 1916)
Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)

defacto.controller: Ottoman Empire (XIII Corps, Ali Ihsan) and German officers, with the returned Persian nationalist government
defacto.note: The Ottomans held Kermanshah from 2 July 1916 until their retreat after the fall of Baghdad (11 March 1917); the exact evacuation date is not established. Verification: Wikipedia ('Battle of Khanaqin') says the Russians occupied Khanaqin after Ali Ihsan was recalled to Baghdad in Feb 1917, so the Ottoman hold on Kermanshah ended between Feb and mid-March 1917; the exact date remains unknown.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kermanshah iv. History to 1953' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kermanshah-04-history-to-1953/)

defacto.controller: Imperial Russia (Baratov's remaining troops, disintegrating after the revolution)
defacto.note: After the Ottoman retreat Russian forces re-entered the Kermanshah area; most Russian troops left Persia between December 1917 and March 1918, a few under Baratov passing into British service. Dates low-confidence.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Russia i. Russo-Iranian Relations up to the Bolshevik Revolution' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/russia-i-relations/)

defacto.controller: British (Dunsterforce lines of communication, then Norperforce)
defacto.note: The British held the Mesopotamia-Kermanshah-Hamadan-Qazvin-Anzali road line; Dunsterville reached Hamadan in Feb 1918. The garrisons were progressively reduced; Norperforce withdrew on 21 April 1921. Persian civil authority continued.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Dunsterforce' (cross-check)

defacto.note: Occupied on 19 June 1838 in response to Mohammad Shah's siege of Herat; the Persians lifted the siege on 9 Sept 1838 but, "owing to the shifty character of their subsequent diplomacy", the island was not evacuated until March 1842.

defacto.note: Occupied 4 Dec 1856; Iranica: held until spring 1858 although the main forces left in 1857.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Anglo-Persian War (1856-57)' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/anglo-persian-war-1856-57/)

defacto.controller: Ka'b sheikhs of Fallahiyeh, then Khaz'al (decrees of 1903 granting Fallahiyeh, Hendijan, Deh Molla and Mashur as perpetual holdings)
defacto.note: The Ka'b heartland and the coastal lands behind Mohammerah were held by Arab sheikhs acknowledging the shah. Pre-1897 holdings and rulers are only loosely characterised here.

defacto.controller: Sheikh Khaz'al (administrator of northern Khuzestan from 1907)
defacto.note: Sardar Mokarram (later Nezam al-Saltaneh) placed Khaz'al in charge of northern Khuzestan in 1907; by 1911 the governorship "does not confer any great powers, most of the country being under the rule of the Shaikh" with only Dezful and Shushtar outside his control.

defacto.controller: Khans of Boir Ahmad (Garmsir/Sardsir), the Noi and other Kuhgiluya khans; Mamasani chief Emamqoli Khan
defacto.note: The tribal khans fell foul of the Qajars (Mohammad-Taher Khan blinded c.1800) but generally ruled their districts under nominal Qajar suzerainty with the Fars governor's backing at times. Tang-e Tamradi (Aug 1930) was a major tribal defeat of Reza Shah's army.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Boir Aḥmadī' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/boir-ahmadi/)

defacto.controller: Boir Ahmad / Kohgiluyeh / Mamasani khans vs. Reza Shah's army
defacto.note: After the Tamradi defeat (heavy losses - Iranica Boir Ahmadi: "said to have exceeded 1,000 casualties"; Fars iv gives about 400 killed; Aug 1930) the khans eventually surrendered and were executed in 1932; a military government then imposed order for the next decade.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Boir Aḥmadī' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/boir-ahmadi/)

defacto.note: After Reza Shah's abdication central authority collapsed locally and tribal politics revived. In 1962-63 two khans resisted land reform, ambushed government forces at Tang-e Gochestan/Gachina Pass and were crushed in June 1963; thereafter the area was under tight security-force control.

defacto.controller: Kurdish groups (KDPI, Komala, local councils) vs. the Islamic Republic
defacto.note: Kurdish forces took the towns and garrisons of Paveh and Marivan region in March 1979; the army retook Paveh in the August 1979 offensive and mountain areas remained insurgent until 1983-84.

defacto.controller: Sayyed Abd al-Hosayn Lari (Najafi Lari), a pro-constitution mujtahid
defacto.note: In 1909 he proclaimed a revolt, issued his own postage stamps (in use March-May 1909) and, per Iranica, "ruled Larestan until the spring of 1915", when the governor-general of Fars sent Habib-Allah Khan Qavam al-Molk to pacify it. Lorimer-based accounts have him driven from Lar and returning in August 1909 and later deported to Shiraz; continuity of control is uncertain.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv' (Sayyed ʿAbd-al-Ḥosayn Lārī 1909-spring 1915) [search extract]

defacto.controller: Qawasim (Qasimi) sheikhs of Lengeh (Sheikh Qazib ibn Rashid last)
defacto.note: The Qasimi sheikh administered Lengeh for the Persian government from about 1789 as revenue collector under the governor of Bastak/Fars. In Feb 1887 Persia created the "Gulf Ports" governorate; in September 1887 the Qasimi governorship was dissolved, Sheikh Qazib was arrested and a Persian garrison landed; Sheikh Mohammad ibn Khalifa briefly seized Lengeh in 1898-99 before Ahmad Khan Daryabeigi retook it in March 1899.

defacto.note: The wali dynasty of Luristan was overthrown in 1796 and replaced at Khorramabad by a governor-general, but the highland tribes kept their own organisation; the Pish-e Kuh was "largely outside control" until Reza Khan's army went in (April 1921 onward).

defacto.note: The army deployed to Luristan in April 1921, took Borujerd (Oct 1923) and Khorramabad (Nov 1923), met a major revolt in May 1924 and the last major engagement in 1926. Wikipedia says direct control came in 1928; Iranica says war dragged on to 1933 but migration was banned from 1929.

defacto.controller: Mukri khans/emirs of Mukriyan as Qajar-appointed hereditary governors (Sauj Bulaq/Mahabad)
defacto.note: Mukriyan, south of Lake Urmia, was ruled by hereditary Mokri khans who served the Qajars as governors of Savojbolagh (Sayf al-Din Khan, d. 1891/2, held the post several times; his son Hosein Khan was killed in the Ottoman attack of 1914). Their power was eroded after Ubeydullah's 1880 invasion: the Qajar state built the Savujbulagh garrison in 1883 (Sayadi 2019: 'a manifestation of the exclusion of the Mukris from the Qajar political power structure'), so 1883 replaces the former 1880-10 placeholder. Not independently dated to the month; some accounts keep Mokri influence into the 1910s.

defacto.controller: Local Kurdish chiefs and the Society for the Revival of Kurdistan (Komala-i Jiyanewey Kurdistan, 1942) under Qazi Muhammad; Soviet zone
defacto.note: After the Iranian army collapsed in Aug-Sept 1941 Kurdish leaders returned and rearmed; Soviet forces held the zone to the north and the Iranian gendarmerie and army were driven out of the Mahabad area. Qazi Muhammad led the Komala (1942) and the KDP (founded Sept 1945). Per British-zone accounts, southern Kurdistan up to Sanandaj was under British occupation, while the Kurdish-held belt from Mahabad to Saqqez lay between the two zones; by 1945 the Iranian government effectively controlled Kurdish areas only south of the Saqqez-Baneh-Sardasht line. defacto.controller: Republic of Mahabad (Qazi Muhammad, president)
defacto.note: Iranica ('Azarbaijan v') has Qazi Muhammad inaugurating the Kurdish Republic at Mahabad on 15 December 1945; Wikipedia gives 22 Jan 1946 for the formal proclamation and presidency. After the Soviets left (May 1946) it was isolated; Iranian troops entered Mahabad on 15-17 Dec 1946.

defacto.note: Qasemlu returned to Mahabad on 20 Oct 1979 as rebels retook the town; in Nov 1979 Kurds held most roads and rural areas. defacto.controller: Nader Mirza Afshar (grandson of Nader Shah), backed by the Afghan rulers of Herat
defacto.note: After Agha Mohammad Khan's death (1797) Nader Mirza returned to Mashhad and styled himself sovereign of Khorasan. Fath-Ali Shah failed in 1799 and 1801, besieged the city in 1802 and Mohammad-Vali Mirza took it in early 1803; Nader was blinded and executed in Tehran. Reach beyond the Mashhad district is not established.

defacto.controller: Mohammad-Hasan Khan Salar (son of Asaf al-Dowleh) with local khans and ulama
defacto.note: Mashhad rose on 25 Aug 1848, just before Mohammad Shah's death in early September, and held out against Hamza Mirza and then Sultan Morad Mirza; besieged from June 1849, it surrendered on 13 or 23 March 1850. Salar was executed on 29 April 1850. Iranica dates the whole revolt c.1847-51; the day-level chronology comes from Wikipedia only.

defacto.note: The Ka'b and later Muhaysin sheikhs "were for two centuries the most powerful chieftains of south-western Persia". Muhammara's allegiance shifted between Persia and the Ottomans.

defacto.note: In 1837 Ali Rida Pasha captured and destroyed Muhammara and the Ka'b paid homage to the Ottomans; the town was "alternately claimed and occupied" until the Second Treaty of Erzurum (31 May 1847), Article II, ceded Mohammerah and Khizr island to Persia. defacto.note: Mohammerah fell on 26-27 March 1857 after naval bombardment; the flotilla reached Ahvaz on 1 April; hostilities ceased about 4 April and the Treaty of Paris was ratified on 2 May. defacto.controller: Muhaysin sheikhs; Sheikh Khaz'al Khan (sheikh from June 1897)
defacto.note: Khaz'al succeeded his assassinated brother Mazal in June 1897, was recognised as Sardar Arfa' (1902), enjoyed British protection (assurances 1899-1908; KCIE 1910/1917) and ruled a "semi-independent realm". On 6 Dec 1924 he submitted to Reza Khan at Ahvaz; he was seized on 18 April 1925 and held in Tehran until his death (27 May 1936). The 1857-97 part of this span is only loosely characterised.

defacto.controller: Sultanate of Muscat and Oman (Al Bu Sa'id) under lease from the Qajar shahs
defacto.note: Under a Persian firman of 1793/94 the Sultan administered Bandar Abbas, the Minab-Khamir coastal strip and the islands of Qeshm and Hormuz for 75 years (garrison of 120 Nubians and 80 Arabs in 1811). Mulla Hosein of Qeshm seized Bandar Abbas after 1804; the Qasimi and the Bombay Marine contested Qeshm c.1806-10. A 1855 accord limited the lease to 20 years at 16,000 tomans a year; the Qajars regained the port in October 1868 amid dynastic trouble in Muscat.

defacto.controller: Ottoman Empire (troops on the orders of the vali of Baghdad, with Sunni Kurdish tribes)
defacto.note: The Ottomans began occupying Persian frontier districts on 23 May 1906 (Behik in Baradost), taking Dasht, Mergever and parts of Sardasht, Bana, Ganjachin and Baradost; Mergever was occupied again on 3 Aug 1907. Pressure by Russia and Britain pushed them back around 1911-12; the withdrawal was incomplete and intermittent. End date is approximate.

defacto.note: Pesyan was made military governor-general by the post-coup government on 2-3 April 1921. After Qavam al-Saltaneh became premier (late May) and sent Najd al-Saltaneh as governor, Pesyan resumed full control in July and defied Tehran until killed fighting Kurdish forces under Sardar Mo'azzaz Bojnurdi at Quchan on 3 Oct 1921. defacto.controller: Valis of Pusht-e Kuh (hereditary Faili Lur 'Vali dynasty': Hoseynqoli Khan Abu Qaddara to c.1900-01, then his son Gholam-Reza Khan, titled Sarim al-Saltaneh/Sardar Ashrafi)
defacto.note: After 1796 the wali family withdrew from Khorramabad to Pusht-e Kuh, where 'quasi-autonomous governors (wali)' ruled until about 1929 (Iranica). Wali names confirmed: Hoseynqoli Khan Abu Qaddara, succeeded around 1900-01 by his son Gholam-Reza Khan, who 'only tacitly acknowledged his vassal status to the Qajars with annual tribute' (hence indirect), held the rank of major-general and fled to Baghdad with his valuables in 1928-29 rather than accept Reza Shah's invitation to Tehran; he died in Baghdad in 1939. The researcher's alternative account (Vali defeated and fleeing to Iraq with Simko in 1922) is contradicted by this chronology and is dropped.

defacto.controller: Khozeimeh 'Alam amirs of Qa'enat (Mir 'Alam Khan Heshmat al-Molk; Amir Esma'il Shawkat al-Molk, to 1904; Amir Mohammad Ebrahim Shawkat al-Molk, governor 1904-1924, then his two nephews, incl. Amir Ma'soum Khan, 'the last ruling amir')

defacto.controller: Qashqai ilkhanis (Jani Khan, ilkhani from 1818/19; Mohammad-Ali Khan 1823-52; Mohammad-Qoli Khan 1852-67/8; Esmail Khan Soulat al-Dowleh from 1904)
defacto.note: The Qashqai ilkhanate controlled Fars' grazing lands and routes, bowing to the shah at times (Mohammad-Ali Khan was held at court in 1836) and dominating Fars during the weak central rule of 1909-21 (1911 civil war with the Qavami; anti-British rising in 1918; Soulat al-Dowleh reinstated as ilkhani by Mosaddeq in late 1920). CORRECTION: the record ended 1929-03, but Iranica says that in 1926 Soulat al-Dowleh and Nasser Khan were summoned to Tehran as deputies and became virtual prisoners, and 'military governors were assigned to the various Qashqai tribes' with conscription and a new tax system - i.e. direct rule 1926-29. Highly variable autonomy; treated as a single phase.

defacto.controller: Qashqai (Soulat al-Dowleh, Nasser Khan, Khosrow Khan) and allied tribes vs. Reza Shah
defacto.note: The 1929 rising began in spring (the Khamseh Baharlu drove officials out of Darab at the end of April and took Fasa on 9 May); on 4 June the Qashqai closed the Bushehr road and then the Isfahan road, isolating Shiraz, which was under siege by mid-June; on 10 July the government flew Soulat al-Dowleh from prison to Shiraz to negotiate; the Khamseh occupied the eastern towns and the Baharlu reached the Kerman frontier; by summer the rebels held 'the whole province of Fars' outside the cities (Iranica 'Fars iv'). It ended with the August 1929 truce and amnesty. CORRECTION: the record previously ran to 1933 as 'contested'; the 1929 truce withdrew the military governors, and the 1932 rebellion 'in vain' is not documented as holding territory (see the next record).

defacto.note: After an attempt to arrest Khosrow Khan in June 1980, Qashqai insurgents "defied the central government" for two years from camps in the mountains until a night attack by the Revolutionary Guards in April 1982; Khosrow Khan was executed on 8 Oct 1982. defacto.note: Formed 16 Sept 1918 from Dunsterforce remnants with its HQ at Qazvin, the main body at Manjil and a battalion at Zanjan; about 6,000 men in 1918, 3,600 by 26 Oct 1920; completely withdrawn into Mesopotamia on 21 April 1921, leaving its arms to the Persian Cossacks. defacto.controller: Za'faranlu Kurdish ilkhanis of Quchan (e.g. Reza-Qoli Khan, defeated by Abbas Mirza in 1832; Sam Khan)
defacto.note: Kurdish khans held the Quchan marches as hereditary governors, fielding thousands of horsemen and acknowledging the shah only intermittently. Reza Khan's bombing of Bojnurd (18 May 1925) opened the end of the Kurdish ilkhani system; end date is therefore a convenience marker, not a precise date for Quchan. Abbas Mirza razed the Quchan fortress and exiled Reza-Qoli Khan after the 1832 battle (13,000 Kurds against 19,000 men); Iranica nonetheless says the Za'faranlu kept their tribal structure and ilkhani leadership throughout the Qajar era (Sam Khan fought for the shah against Salar and at Herat), and that Chenaran and Darreh Gaz were 'from time to time' under the governor of Khorasan's direct rule. defacto.controller: Shahsevan tribal khans ("the time of the independent khans")
defacto.note: Russia closed the Moghan frontier to the Shahsevan in 1884 and between 1884 and 1922 the Shahsevan operated with minimal central authority. They were among the first major tribes pacified and disarmed by Reza Khan's army in winter-spring 1922-23. Status before 1884 (Qajar-appointed governors with tribal chiefs) is not recorded here. Verification (Iranica 'Shahsevan'): 'virtually independent of central government for nearly four decades'; the chiefs 'usually controlled the region ... focused on the city of Ardabil and smaller urban centers' until Reza Khan's army pacified them in winter-spring 1922-23; a Russian force of 5,000 under Gen. Fidarov campaigned against them in 1912. 'none' is kept because Iranica does not describe an acknowledgment of the shah, but 'indirect' is arguable.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Shahsevan' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/shahsevan/)

defacto.controller: Ismail Agha "Simko" of the Shikak (base at Chehriq castle)
defacto.note: Simko established authority west of Lake Urmia in 1918-19, plundered Urmia in winter 1920, defeated government forces at Tasuj (March 1921) and was joined in summer 1921 by the Mamash, Mangur and Piran. He was defeated by Reza Khan's army in summer 1922 and fled to Iraq; he returned and rebelled again in 1926 and was killed on 30 June 1930 at Ushnu. Persian authority existed only in a few towns.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Čahrīq' (iranicaonline.org) and 'Khiābāni'/'Great Britain v' extracts on Simko 1920-22 [search extracts]

defacto.controller: Simko and the Shikak
defacto.note: Wikipedia (single source) places Mahabad (Sauj Bulaq) in Simko's hands after the death of Maj. Malakzadeh and about 600 gendarmes in October 1921, with control extending to Sardasht and Baneh by 1922. Treat as low-confidence.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Local Sistani chiefs (Sarbandi, Kayani maliks; Ali Khan Sarbandi) with Persian and Afghan claims overlapping
defacto.note: Sistan was disputed between Persia and Afghan rulers and run by local chiefs. Ali Khan accepted Persian allegiance in 1857, unpopularly. The Goldsmid arbitration of 1872 awarded Persian (west) Sistan to Persia; Persian governors followed from December 1873.
sources: Qatar Digital Library, 'Military Report on Persian Seistan' and 'Seistan arbitration case' (British Library IOR; qdl.qa) [search extracts]

defacto.controller: Persian governors with the 'Alam amirs of Qa'enat (Mir 'Alam Khan, then Shawkat al-Molk)
defacto.note: Iranica: Mir 'Alam Khan drove insurgents out of Sistan and added it to his Qa'enat amirate under Naser al-Din Shah. Sistanis rebelled against the Qa'en chief in Dec 1872 (shut him in Nasirabad); a Persian governor (Samsam al-Mulk, then Mohammad Ja'far Khan, Dec 1873) followed.
sources: Qatar Digital Library, 'Military Report on Persian Seistan' and 'Seistan arbitration case' (British Library IOR; qdl.qa) [search extracts]

defacto.controller: British India: East Persia Cordon (July 1915), Seistan Force (from March 1916; commander Col. J. M. Wilkeley, then R. E. H. Dyer from Feb 1916)
defacto.note: British-Indian troops held Sistan to bar German agents from Afghanistan; the Persian governor remained but the force dominated Nasratabad and the border. The cordon later extended north via Birjand to Mashhad and (from 1918) to the Transcaspian line. Last elements left Persia in November 1920.

defacto.controller: 'Alam amirs of Qa'enat as governors of Sistan
defacto.note: After the British withdrawal the Alam family governed Sistan and Qa'enat as quasi-hereditary governors: Shawkat al-Molk had full authority in 1921 and resigned in 1924 in favour of two nephews (Iranica). Weakly documented; the 1935 end is a marker only.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'ʿAlam, Moḥammad Ebrāhim, Amir Šawkat-al-Molk' (https://iranicaonline.org/articles/alam-mohammad-ebrahim-amir-sawkat-al-molk) [search extract]

defacto.controller: British-officered South Persia Rifles (Sir Percy Sykes) with Indian Army support
defacto.note: Sykes landed at Bandar Abbas in March 1916 to raise the South Persia Rifles (authorised strength 11,000; about 3,300 infantry and 450 cavalry by mid-1917); the force was disbanded in 1921 after the coup. Persian civil governors remained. Whether this deserves the occupation label is debatable (the Qajar government assented under pressure). Verification: this record now covers Bandar Abbas only; Kerman (from June 1916) and Shiraz (from Nov 1916) have their own records.

defacto.controller: Hereditary governors of Tabas (Mir Hasan Khan 'Vakil-i-Tabas' family; Zangu'i khans; Haji Mohammad Baqer Khan 'Emad al-Molk' under Naser al-Din Shah)
defacto.note: Per the Gazetteer of Persia vol. I (c.1910) the Tabas governorship was hereditary: Nader Shah gave the district to 'Ali Murad Khan of the Zangu'i (Arab, related to the Khozeima amirs of Qa'en) and 'the same family still govern[s] the district'; the older Vakil-i-Tabas family also held it. Haji Mohammad Baqer Khan 'Emad al-Molk' (d. 1894) was succeeded by his eldest son 'Ali Akbar Khan. The khan paid a fixed sum to the shah and was otherwise left to do much as he pleased. The family was still in office around 1910, so the end cannot be earlier; no source for its end was found and 1935 stays a placeholder tied to Pahlavi centralisation.
sources: Gazetteer of Persia vol. I (Government of India, c.1910), via Qatar Digital Library (qdl.qa): Tabas governorship hereditary in the family of Mir Hasan Khan 'Vakil-i-Tabas' [search extract]; also Iranica 'Khorasan xi' extract naming the Zangu'i khans of Tabas
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Khorasan xi. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/khorasan-xi-history-in-the-qajar-and-pahlavi-periods/)

defacto.controller: Anjoman of Tabriz and constitutionalist fighters (Sattar Khan, Baqer Khan)
defacto.note: Tabriz refused Mohammad Ali Shah's coup of 23 June 1908 and withstood a royalist siege for ten months until Russian troops entered on 30 April 1909. The city sought to restore the constitution, not to secede.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Russian occupation of Tabriz' (23 June 1908 rebellion date; cross-check)
Wikipedia, 'Russian occupation of Tabriz' (cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915)

defacto.controller: Imperial Russia (General Snarski's expeditionary force; later Russian garrisons in Tabriz and along the Julfa road)
defacto.note: Russian troops held Tabriz from 30 April 1909; after the Fedayeen attack of 21 Dec 1911 Russia re-entered after shelling on 31 Dec 1911 and executed about 1,200. Russia evacuated on 17 Dec 1914 and the Ottomans (Kurdish irregulars and regulars) held Tabriz 8-31 Jan 1915 (under a month) before Russia returned; last Russians left 28 Feb 1918. Iranian administration continued throughout.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Russian occupation of Tabriz' (cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Russia i. Russo-Iranian Relations up to the Bolshevik Revolution' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/russia-i-relations/)

defacto.controller: Ottoman Empire (IV Corps)
defacto.note: Ottoman forces entered Tabriz on 8 June 1918 (Wikipedia's other date: 18 June) and left after the Armistice of Mudros (30 Oct 1918); exact evacuation date not established.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)
Wikipedia, 'Russian occupation of Tabriz' (cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915)

defacto.controller: Khans of Tangestan, Dashtestan and Dashti (Zair Khidr, Shaikh Hosein Khan of Chah Kutah) under the governor of Bushehr
defacto.note: Tribal khans of the Bushehr hinterland controlled their districts and acknowledged the Qajars loosely. Baseline characterisation only.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Rais-Ali Delvari' and 'British occupation of Bushehr' (cross-check)
Not independently verified in this research pass; reconstructed from general scholarship

defacto.controller: Tangestani/Dashti tribal forces (Rais Ali Delvari, killed 2 Sept 1915; Shaikh Hosein Khan Chahkutahi; Zair Khidr) with German agent Wassmuss vs. the British and pro-British khans
defacto.note: The tribes attacked the British Residency at Bushehr on 12 July 1915, fought the British after the occupation of Bushehr (8 Aug 1915) and kept the hinterland in revolt, joined by the Qashqai in 1918, until the rising subsided (influenza, British pressure). Some sources say Tangestani resistance lasted to 1921.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Rais-Ali Delvari' and 'British occupation of Bushehr' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fārs iv. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fars-iv/)

defacto.controller: Qara'i khans: Eshaq Khan (strangled 8 July 1816) then his son Mohammad Khan (1816-32)
defacto.note: Eshaq Khan Qara'i ruled Torbat-e Heydarieh as a quasi-independent magnate under Fath-Ali Shah (at times effective master of Mohammad-Vali Mirza's Khorasan). Abbas Mirza captured Mohammad Khan by trickery in 1832, ending Qara'i independence; afterwards Qajar-appointed governors ruled.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Esḥāq Khan Qarāʾī' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/eshaq-qarai/) [search extract]
Wikipedia, 'Eshaq Khan Qaraei-Torbati' (cross-check; 8 July 1816 death)
Wikipedia, 'Mohammad Khan Qaraei-Torbati' (cross-check; rule 1816-32, capture 1832)

defacto.controller: Yomut and Goklen (Guklan) tribal leaders
defacto.note: Turkmen of the Gorgan plain raided Khorasan and Astarabad and beat Persian armies (1858 near Qarri-qal'a; 1860 at Merv). Qajar governors of Astarabad held the town and a few forts; the plain itself was outside effective Persian control. Some Goklen paid taxes or migrated under pressure.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Gorgān vii. History from the Safavids to the end of the Pahlavi era' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/gorgan-vii/)

Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Guklān' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/guklan/)

defacto.controller: Turkmen tribal chiefs under nominal Persian governors of Astarabad (Persian posts, tax-collection, Russian border pressure)
defacto.note: After the Russian conquest of the Akhal Teke and the Akhal-Khorasan convention (1881) the Yomut/Goklen lost their steppe hinterland and were drawn into limited Persian tax/administrative arrangements. Reza Khan's army moved in and disarmed the Turkmen in 1925; Gonbad-e Qabus became the settlement centre. The 1881 start is a convenience marker.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Gorgān vii. History from the Safavids to the end of the Pahlavi era' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/gorgan-vii/)

defacto.controller: Turkmen People's Councils / Turkmen Cultural and Political Society vs. IRGC
defacto.note: After the Revolution Turkmen councils (shuras) ran local affairs; open clashes in March 1979 ended in a ceasefire on 3 April, with renewed fighting in May and August 1979 and in February 1980; by early 1980 the IRGC had occupied the Turkmen towns. The councils did not secede, and control of towns flipped; included for completeness at low confidence.
sources: Wikipedia, '1979 Turkmen rebellion in Iran' and '1979 Iranian ethnic unrest' (cross-check; no better source found)
Wikipedia, '1979 Iranian ethnic unrest' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Sheikh Ubeydullah of Nehri and his Kurdish tribal host (Ottoman and Iranian Kurds) vs. Qajar forces from Tabriz
defacto.note: Tens of thousands of Kurds crossed into north-west Persia in autumn 1880, took Sauj Bulaq (Mahabad) and Maragheh, failed to take Urmia (its Shia population refused to surrender) and withdrew after about eight weeks. Exact start/end dates not fixed in the sources consulted. Verification: Wikipedia ('Uprising of Sheikh Ubeydullah') says Ubeydullah's son Abdulqadir 'retreated to Mahabad, which they held for a few days' before Qajar forces from Tabriz arrived, and that after about eight weeks the rebels retreated; Urmia held out. Control was transient and set up no administration, so the status is changed from 'none' to 'contested' (low).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Uprising of Sheikh Ubeydullah' (cross-check; ~8 weeks, Mahabad and Maragheh taken, Urmia held out)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, extract on Sheikh Ubeydullah's 1298/1880 invasion of Azarbaijan (iranicaonline.org, 'Kurdish language ii' / 'Safavid dynasty (cont.)' search results)
Wikipedia, 'Uprising of Sheikh Ubeydullah' (cross-check; Mahabad held a few days; withdrawal after eight weeks)

defacto.controller: Assyrian/Armenian forces, Simko's Shikak and local Persian notables after Russia's withdrawal
defacto.note: Russian troops left Azerbaijan between Jan and March 1918. Simko murdered the Assyrian patriarch Mar Shimun on 3 March 1918; Assyrians, Armenians and Kurds fought for the Urmia plain until the Ottomans arrived. Control was fragmented and short-lived.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Russia i. Russo-Iranian Relations up to the Bolshevik Revolution' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/russia-i-relations/)
Wikipedia, 'Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Ottoman Empire (IV Corps)
defacto.note: Dilman (Salmas) fell on 18 June and Urmia on 31 July 1918; Ottoman forces left after the Armistice of Mudros (30 Oct 1918).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Persian campaign (World War I)' (cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations)

defacto.controller: United Kingdom (Persia and Iraq Force), later joined by the US Persian Gulf Command (from Dec 1942) in Khuzestan
defacto.note: British forces entered Khuzestan, took Abadan and the Ahvaz oilfields and advanced from Iraq via Kermanshah to Hamadan in Aug-Sept 1941. Iranian administration continued. The Allies withdrew from Tehran on 17 Oct 1941; British (and US) troops left by 2 March 1946 under the Tripartite Treaty.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran' (cross-check)
Wikipedia, 'Iran crisis of 1946' (cross-check)
Kurdistan Chronicle, 'Soviet Union's Politics Toward the Iranian Kurds' (kurdistanchronicle.com/babat/2718) [search extract]

defacto.controller: Soviet Union (44th and 47th Armies)
defacto.note: Soviet troops took Tabriz and Ardabil by 26 Aug 1941. Iranian civil administration continued; the Tripartite Treaty (29 Jan 1942) declared the presence not an occupation and required withdrawal within six months of the end of hostilities (2 March 1946).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Azarbaijan v. History from 1941 to 1947' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/azerbaijan-v/)

defacto.controller: Azerbaijan People's Government (Democratic Party of Azerbaijan; Ja'far Pishevari, premier) under Soviet protection
defacto.note: The Democrats took Tabriz around 20-21 Nov 1945 and proclaimed the Autonomous Government of Azerbaijan on 12 Dec 1945 while Soviet troops blocked the Iranian army. Soviet forces left in May 1946; Iranian forces began moving in on 9 Dec 1946 and entered Tabriz on 12-13 Dec 1946, when Pishevari fled to Baku. Dating: Iranica ('Azarbaijan v') says all major routes into the province were seized by the Democrats by 19 Nov 1945, an Iranian column of 1,500 troops was stopped at Qazvin by the Soviets, and Tabriz was 'in the hands of the Democratic Party' by 10 Dec 1945; Wikipedia has 21 Nov. The Soviet-held zone therefore reached the Qazvin line. The Zanjan province units were included by the original researcher; Iranica does not name Zanjan, so their inclusion is unverified (the Iranian advance of Dec 1946 is said to have moved on Zanjan, but no source was found here).
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Azarbaijan v. History from 1941 to 1947' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/azerbaijan-v/)
Wikipedia, 'Iran crisis of 1946' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Soviet Union (based at Mashhad and Bojnurd)
defacto.note: Soviet troops entered Khorasan on 3 Shahrivar 1320 (25 Aug 1941) from Sarakhs, Dargaz and Bajgiran and occupied the north-east, based at Mashhad and Bojnurd; Iranian civil administration continued. CORRECTION: Iranica ('Khorasan xi') says the Soviets stayed 'until the winter of 1943', but the Soviet communique of 25 Feb 1946 announced that evacuation of 'Meshed, Shahrud and Semnan' would begin on 2 March 1946, and on 24-25 March the Soviets (via Kennan, FRUS) said it 'has already been finished' (Mossadegh doubted this on 3-4 March). 'Winter of 1943' is probably a mis-conversion of winter 1324 Sh. (1945-46). The end date is the Soviet claim of completion; the south-east (Birjand, Tabas) was not in the Soviet zone.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Khorasan xi. History in the Qajar and Pahlavi Periods' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/khorasan-xi-history-in-the-qajar-and-pahlavi-periods/)

defacto.controller: Soviet Union
defacto.note: Soviet forces took Gilan (Anzali, Rasht), Mazandaran and Gorgan in August 1941 and reached Qazvin; they entered Tehran on 17 Sept 1941 and withdrew from it by 17 Oct. Iranian civil administration continued. The last Soviet troops left on about 6-9 May 1946. Verification: Semnan province was split into i_wwii_soviet_semnan (evacuated by 24 March 1946); this record now covers Gilan, Mazandaran, Golestan and Qazvin, held to about 6-9 May 1946.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran' (cross-check)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Azarbaijan v. History from 1941 to 1947' (https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/azerbaijan-v/)
Wikipedia, 'Iran crisis of 1946' (cross-check)

defacto.controller: Baluch chiefs of Sarhad (Rigi, Ismailzai, Damani, Baranzai) who had come to terms with the Persian governor of Bampur; Persian officials at Bampur, Khash and Nasratabad
defacto.note: Gazetteer of Persia vol. IV (c.1908-10): the power of the Sarhad chiefs 'continued almost undiminished', although 'within the last few years' they had submitted to the Persian governor of Bampur, and a small Persian party from Bampur, Khash or Nasratabad could pass through Sarhad levying taxes or blackmail on chiefs and headmen. That is acknowledgment of the shah's governor by local chiefs (indirect), not the total absence of state authority the researcher's 'none' implied. Koyagi: Qajar presence 'waned significantly' after 1906, leaving a vacuum that raiding exploited. The 1850-1900 stretch is weakly documented (Persian garrison at Bampur from 1850) and may have been 'none'; the status here is a low-confidence compromise. Frontier demarcated 1895-96.
sources: Gazetteer of Persia vol. IV (Government of India, c.1908-10), via Qatar Digital Library (qdl.qa) [search extract]

defacto.controller: Soviet Union
defacto.note: Soviet forces held Semnan province (Shahrud, Damghan, Semnan) on the Tehran-Mashhad route from the August 1941 invasion; Iranian civil administration continued. Evacuation of Shahrud and Semnan began on 2 March 1946 and was reported finished by 24-25 March (FRUS 1946 VII, doc. 282). Split from the other Soviet-held provinces, which were evacuated until about 6-9 May 1946.
sources: FRUS 1946 vol. VII, doc. 282, Kennan to Secretary of State, 25 Mar 1946 (history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1946v07/d282): Soviet statement that evacuation of Meshed, Shahrud and Semnan, begun 2 Mar 1946, was finished
